## Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Identify the **three main node types** in a causal diagram and know when to use each
- Assign **signed directed links** [+]/[-] to represent how one variable influences another
- Recognize the three fundamental **triplet structures**: chain, fork, and collider
- Apply **d-separation** rules to determine when information flows (or stops) between variables
- Build a complete **qualitative DAG** for Rwanda's maternal and newborn health system
:::

# From Intuition to Structure {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Why writing down your causal beliefs changes everything</span>


## Everyone Has a Mental Model

You already carry causal beliefs around in your head.

. . .

"If we train more community health workers, outcomes will improve." "Insurance coverage drives facility delivery rates." "Better equipment leads to better care."

These are causal claims. The problem? They live in your head, where nobody can challenge them.

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Everyone has a mental model. The question is whether yours is written down where others can challenge it.**
:::


## Implicit vs. Explicit Models

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Implicit Models (in your head)**

- Vague and shifting
- Hidden assumptions
- Two people disagree without knowing *why*
- Cannot be tested against data
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Explicit Models (on paper)**

- Precise and shareable
- Assumptions are visible
- Disagreements become *productive*
- Generate testable predictions
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
A qualitative causal model is just a disciplined way of writing down what you believe about how things connect — before you add any numbers.
:::


## The Model-Building Process

<div class="step-flow">
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #005CB9;"><span class="step-number">1</span><br>List your<br>variables</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #83BD00;"><span class="step-number green">2</span><br>Classify<br>node types</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #FA7650;"><span class="step-number orange">3</span><br>Draw<br>arrows</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #F8A623;"><span class="step-number amber">4</span><br>Assign<br>signs</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #3E9B6E;"><span class="step-number teal">5</span><br>Check<br>structure</div>
</div>

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[Everyday Example]{.example-label}

A school principal says: "I think class size affects teacher attention, and teacher attention affects test scores." That sentence *is* a causal model: **Class Size → Teacher Attention → Test Scores** with signs [-] and [+]. We just gave it structure.
:::


# Three Node Types {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">The building blocks of every causal diagram</span>


## Probabilistic Nodes (Ovals)

::: {.definition-box}
**Probabilistic Node:** A variable whose value is uncertain — determined by nature or upstream causes. You observe it but do not directly control it. Drawn as an **oval**.
:::

Think of it this way: these are the things the world throws at you.

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**Everyday:** Tomorrow's weather, a student's exam score, traffic on your commute
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.example-block}
[MNH Example]{.example-label}

- **Quality of Care** {Good, Poor}
- **Care-Seeking Behavior** {High, Low}
- **Workforce Competency** {Competent, Developing}
:::
:::
:::

<table style="width: 70%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">Quality<br>of Care</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">Care-Seeking<br>Behavior</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">Workforce<br>Competency</div></td>
</tr>
</table>


## Decision Nodes (Rectangles)

::: {.definition-box}
**Decision Node:** A variable you *choose*. It represents a deliberate action by a decision-maker. Drawn as a **rectangle**.
:::

Think of it this way: these are the levers you can pull.

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**Everyday:** Which university to apply to, how much to spend on advertising, whether to study or watch TV
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.example-block}
[MNH Example]{.example-label}

- **CHW Training Investment** {Fund, Don't Fund}
- **Equipment Procurement** {Invest, Defer}
- **Health Insurance Coverage** {Expand Mutuelle de Santé (Rwanda's community health insurance), Keep As Is}
:::
:::
:::

<table style="width: 70%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">CHW Training<br>Investment</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">Equipment<br>Procurement</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">Insurance<br>Policy</div></td>
</tr>
</table>


## Objective Nodes (Hexagons)

::: {.definition-box}
**Objective Node:** The thing you are ultimately trying to achieve. Drawn as a **hexagon**. Arrows flow *into* objective nodes, never *out*. This is the scoreboard.
:::

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**Everyday:** Your final GPA, a company's annual profit, a team's win-loss record
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.example-block}
[MNH Example]{.example-label}

- **Neonatal Mortality** — Rwanda NMR ~16 per 1,000
- **Maternal Mortality** — Rwanda MMR ~248 per 100,000
:::
:::
:::

<table style="width: 50%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="padding: 0.5em 1em; border-style: double;">Neonatal<br>Mortality</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="padding: 0.5em 1em; border-style: double;">Maternal<br>Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
</table>


## Node Types: Quick Reference

| Type | Shape | What it represents | Who controls it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Probabilistic** | Oval | Uncertain variables | Nature / context |
| **Decision** | Rectangle | Choices you make | The decision-maker |
| **Objective** | Hexagon | Goals you're trying to achieve | Nobody — it's the outcome |

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**A note on function nodes:** There is a fourth type — function nodes — for variables calculated exactly from their parents (like "Total Spending = Training + Equipment + Systems"). We will not focus on them here. Just know they exist for accounting identities and formulas.
:::


# Signed Links {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Arrows that tell you which direction things move</span>


## How Links Work

::: {.definition-box}
**Directed Link:** An arrow from A to B means changing A can change B. The sign — [+] or [-] — tells you the direction.
:::

| Sign | Meaning | Plain English |
|---|---|---|
| **[+]** | More A leads to more B | "A pushes B up" |
| **[-]** | More A leads to less B | "A pushes B down" |

<table style="width: 70%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.6em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect">CHW Training<br>Investment</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node">Workforce<br>Competency</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><span class="dag-arrow negative" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [-]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="border-style: double;">Neonatal<br>Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

Read it out loud: "Training investment *increases* workforce competency, and higher competency *decreases* neonatal mortality."


## Sign Multiplication Along Paths

Here is the trick: when you follow a path through multiple arrows, you multiply the signs.

::: {.callout-box}
**Sign multiplication:** [+] x [+] = [+], [-] x [-] = [+], [+] x [-] = [-]. Same rule as multiplying positive and negative numbers.
:::

| Path | Signs | Overall | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training → Competency → Mortality | [+] x [-] | **[-]** | Training reduces mortality |
| Insurance → Care-Seeking → Quality → Mortality | [+] x [+] x [-] | **[-]** | Insurance reduces mortality |

::: {.example-block}
[Everyday Example]{.example-label}

**Rain → Wet Roads → Car Accidents.** Rain *increases* wet roads [+]. Wet roads *increase* accidents [+]. Overall: [+] x [+] = [+]. Rain increases accidents.
:::


# The Three Triplets {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Every causal diagram is built from just three patterns</span>


## Why Three Triplets Matter

Every DAG — no matter how large — is built from combinations of just three structures. Learn these three patterns and you understand every causal diagram.

| # | Name | Shape | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Chain** (Serial) | A → B → C | B is a *mediator* |
| 2 | **Fork** (Diverging) | A ← B → C | B is a *common cause* |
| 3 | **Collider** (Converging) | A → B ← C | B is a *collision point* |

::: {.callout-box .orange}
Each triplet has its own rule about when information flows and when it stops. Get these rules wrong and your entire analysis falls apart.
:::


## Triplet 1: The Chain

::: {.definition-box}
**Chain:** A → B → C. Node B sits in the middle, passing information from A to C. B is a **mediator**.
:::

::: {.example-block}
[Everyday Example]{.example-label}

**Rain → Wet Roads → Car Accidents.** If you already know the roads are wet, does learning it rained tell you anything new about accident risk? No. The road condition already captured everything rain had to say.
:::

<table style="width: 60%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.6em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node treatment" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">A</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">→</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">B</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">→</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node outcome" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">C</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

**The rule:** Information flows from A to C through B. But if you **hold B fixed** (condition on it), the flow **stops**.


## Chain: MNH Example

<table style="width: 80%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect">CHW Training<br>Investment</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node">Workforce<br>Competency</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow negative" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [-]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="border-style: double;">Neonatal<br>Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Not conditioning on Competency:**

Training and Mortality are associated. Knowing a district invested in training tells us mortality is likely lower.
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Conditioning on Competency:**

If we already know a health worker is competent, it does not matter *how* she got there. The path is **blocked**.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-box}
**For Rwanda:** Training's value is entirely *mediated* through competency. If you can measure competency directly, you do not need training records to predict outcomes.
:::


## Triplet 2: The Fork

::: {.definition-box}
**Fork:** A ← B → C. Node B is a **common cause** of both A and C. This creates a *spurious correlation* between A and C.
:::

::: {.example-block}
[Everyday Example]{.example-label}

**Ice Cream Sales ← Summer Heat → Drowning Deaths.** Ice cream and drowning are correlated. But ice cream does not cause drowning. Summer heat drives both. Know the temperature, and the link vanishes.
:::

<table style="width: 60%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.6em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node treatment" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">A</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">←</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node confounder" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">B</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">→</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node outcome" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">C</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

**The rule:** A and C look associated, but only because of B. **Hold B fixed**, and A and C become independent.


## Fork: MNH Example

<table style="width: 80%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node">CHW<br>Deployment</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">← [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node confounder">Disease<br>Burden</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="border-style: double;">Neonatal<br>Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Naive observation:**

Districts with more CHWs have *higher* mortality. Health workers cause harm?
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Causal reality:**

Disease burden is the common cause. High-burden districts get more workers *and* have higher mortality. Control for burden and the spurious link disappears.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-box}
**For Rwanda:** Across 30 districts, the Ministry of Health deploys more CHWs to higher-burden areas. Any comparison of CHW density vs. mortality *must* control for baseline disease burden.
:::


## Triplet 3: The Collider

::: {.definition-box}
**Collider:** A → B ← C. Two arrows *collide* at B. This is the dangerous exception — it behaves **opposite** to chains and forks.
:::

::: {.example-block}
[Everyday Example]{.example-label}

**High Grades → University Admission ← Athletic Talent.** A selective university requires high grades or athletic talent. Among *admitted students*, non-athletes must be academic stars. This negative link only appears once you condition on admission.
:::

<table style="width: 60%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.6em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node treatment" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">A</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">→</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 1em; border-width: 3px;">B</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 2em;">←</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;"><div class="dag-node outcome" style="padding: 0.5em 1em;">C</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

**The rule:** A and C are **independent** by default — the collider *blocks* information. But if you **condition on B**, the path **opens**. This is called "explaining away."


## Collider: MNH Example

<table style="width: 80%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node treatment">Staffing<br>Level</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node" style="border-width: 3px;">Quality<br>of Care</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive" style="font-size: 1.8em;">← [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;"><div class="dag-node treatment">Equipment<br>Availability</div></td>
</tr>
</table>

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Not conditioning on Quality:**

Staffing and Equipment are independent — separate decisions.
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Conditioning on Quality = Good:**

Among good-quality facilities, if staffing is low, equipment *must* be excellent. Each cause "explains away" the other.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-box}
**For Rwanda:** With ~1.3 nurses per 1,000 (vs. WHO target of 4.45), if you only study high-performing facilities, staffing and equipment will appear negatively related — a statistical illusion from collider bias.
:::


# Information Flow Rules {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">d-Separation: when does information flow, and when does it stop?</span>


## The Three Rules

Burn this into your memory:

| # | Structure | Default | Condition on middle node |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Chain:** A → B → C | Flows | **BLOCKED** |
| **2** | **Fork:** A ← B → C | Flows | **BLOCKED** |
| **3** | **Collider:** A → B ← C | **BLOCKED** | Flows! |

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
Chains and forks behave the same — conditioning on the middle *blocks* the flow. Colliders are the rebel — conditioning on the middle *opens* the flow.
:::

::: {.callout-box}
**The fancy name:** These rules are called **d-separation** (the "d" stands for directional). Two variables are d-separated if every path between them is blocked. D-separated variables are independent — knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
:::


## Applying d-Separation

In a real diagram, two variables may be connected by *multiple* paths. You must check every path.

::: {.definition-box}
**d-Separation:** X and Y are d-separated given a set Z if **every** path between them is blocked. A path is blocked if it contains: (1) a chain or fork whose middle node is in Z, OR (2) a collider whose middle node (and descendants) is *not* in Z.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Shortcut:** Walk along each path. At each node ask: chain/fork middle, or collider? Chain/fork middle conditioned on → blocked. Collider *not* conditioned on → blocked. One blocked node is enough to block the whole path.
:::


## d-Separation: Worked Example

<table style="width: 75%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.5em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect">Training</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node" style="border-width: 3px;">Quality</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow negative">→ [-]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="border-style: double;">Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
<tr><td></td><td></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">↑ [+]</span></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td></td><td></td><td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node treatment">Equipment</div></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
</table>

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**Q: Training indep. of Mortality given Quality?**

Path: Training → Quality → Mortality. Quality is a **chain** middle, conditioned on → **Blocked**. Answer: **Yes**, d-separated.
:::
::: {.col}
**Q: Training indep. of Equipment given Quality?**

Path: Training → Quality ← Equipment. Quality is a **collider**, conditioned on → **Opened**. Answer: **No**, not d-separated.
:::
:::


# MNH Application: Rwanda {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Building a qualitative DAG with real-world structure</span>


## Rwanda at a Glance

| Indicator | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Neonatal Mortality Rate | ~16 per 1,000 live births | WHO |
| Maternal Mortality Ratio | ~248 per 100,000 live births | WHO |
| Facility delivery rate | 94%+ | DHS |
| Health insurance (Mutuelle de Sante) | ~85% coverage | Gov't of Rwanda |
| Nurses per 1,000 population | ~1.3 (WHO target: 4.45) | WHO |
| Community health workers | ~58,000 across 30 districts | Gov't of Rwanda |

::: {.callout-box}
Rwanda's CHW program and Mutuelle de Sante universal insurance are widely studied success stories. But challenges remain: the workforce is stretched thin, and neonatal mortality has been harder to reduce than under-5 mortality.
:::


## Choosing Our Variables

We want a DAG rich enough to capture key dynamics but small enough to reason about — 7 nodes:

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**Decision Nodes (Rectangles)**

- **CHW Training Investment**
- **Equipment Procurement**
- **Insurance Policy** (Mutuelle)
:::
::: {.col}
**Probabilistic Nodes (Ovals)**

- **Workforce Competency**
- **Equipment Availability**
- **Care-Seeking Behavior**
- **Quality of Care**

**Objective Node (Hexagon)**

- **Neonatal Mortality**
:::
:::


## The Rwanda MNH DAG

<table style="width: 95%; margin: 0.3em auto; font-size: 0.45em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">CHW Training<br>Investment</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
<td rowspan="3" style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">Workforce<br>Competency</div></td>
<td rowspan="3" style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
<td rowspan="3" style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em; border-width: 3px;">Quality<br>of Care</div></td>
<td rowspan="3" style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow negative">→ [-]</span></td>
<td rowspan="3" style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node hexagon outcome" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em; border-style: double;">Neonatal<br>Mortality</div></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">Equipment<br>Procurement</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">Equipment<br>Availability</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">Insurance<br>Policy</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.4em;"><div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.4em 0.6em;">Care-Seeking<br>Behavior</div></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><span class="dag-arrow positive">→ [+]</span></td>
</tr>
</table>

::: {.callout-box}
Read left to right: **Decisions** (what we control) → **Mediators** (how they work) → **Quality of Care** (the bottleneck) → **Neonatal Mortality** (what we want to reduce).
:::


## Signs and Path Analysis

| Link | Sign | Why |
|---|---|---|
| CHW Training → Workforce Competency | [+] | Trained CHWs are more skilled |
| Equipment Procurement → Equipment Availability | [+] | Procurement puts equipment in facilities |
| Insurance Policy → Care-Seeking Behavior | [+] | Mutuelle removes financial barriers |
| Workforce Competency → Quality of Care | [+] | Competent workers deliver better care |
| Equipment Availability → Quality of Care | [+] | Equipment enables clinical interventions |
| Care-Seeking Behavior → Quality of Care | [+] | Higher utilization enables systematic improvement |
| Quality of Care → Neonatal Mortality | [-] | Better care saves newborn lives |

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Overall path signs:** Every decision-to-mortality path carries [-]. All three channels reduce mortality. The question is: **which has the strongest effect?** Chapter 4 will answer that.
:::


## Spotting Triplets in the Rwanda DAG

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Chains**

- Training → Competency → Quality
- Insurance → Care-Seeking → Quality
- Procurement → Availability → Quality → Mortality

*Conditioning on the mediator blocks the path.*
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Colliders**

- Competency → Quality ← Availability
- Competency → Quality ← Care-Seeking

*Quality is a collider. Conditioning on it creates spurious links between its parents — "explaining away."*
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**No fork in this DAG?** Correct — each decision is a separate root node. Adding "Total Health Budget" as parent of all three decisions would create forks (Training ← Budget → Equipment).
:::


# R Workshop {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Building Rwanda's DAG in R with dagitty and ggdag</span>


## Setting Up

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true

# Install packages (run once — uncomment the line below)
# install.packages(c("dagitty", "ggdag", "ggplot2"))

library(dagitty)    # Define and analyze DAGs
library(ggdag)      # Visualize DAGs using ggplot2
library(ggplot2)    # General plotting
```


## Step 1: Define Rwanda's DAG

```{r}
#| label: define-dag
#| echo: true

# Rwanda MNH Qualitative DAG
# 7 nodes: 3 decisions, 3 probabilistic, 1 objective
rwanda_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  # Decision nodes (things we control)
  CHW_Training       [pos="0,0"]
  Equipment_Procure  [pos="0,1"]
  Insurance_Policy   [pos="0,2"]

  # Probabilistic nodes (uncertain, nature-determined)
  Competency         [pos="1,0"]
  Equip_Avail        [pos="1,1"]
  Care_Seeking       [pos="1,2"]
  Quality            [pos="2,1"]

  # Objective node (what we want to reduce)
  Neonatal_Mortality [pos="3,1"]

  # Causal arrows
  CHW_Training      -> Competency
  Equipment_Procure -> Equip_Avail
  Insurance_Policy  -> Care_Seeking
  Competency        -> Quality
  Equip_Avail       -> Quality
  Care_Seeking      -> Quality
  Quality           -> Neonatal_Mortality
}')

isAcyclic(rwanda_dag)   # Should return TRUE
```


## Step 2: Visualize the DAG

```{r}
#| label: visualize-dag
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Basic plot
ggdag(rwanda_dag) +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title    = "Rwanda MNH: Qualitative Causal Model",
       subtitle = "7-node DAG for neonatal health investment")

# Color-coded by exposure and outcome
ggdag_status(rwanda_dag,
             exposure = "CHW_Training",
             outcome  = "Neonatal_Mortality") +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title = "Exposure: CHW Training | Outcome: Neonatal Mortality")
```


## Step 3: Test d-Separation

```{r}
#| label: dsep-tests
#| echo: true

# Test 1: Training indep of Mortality given Quality? (chain)
dseparated(rwanda_dag,
           "CHW_Training", "Neonatal_Mortality", "Quality")
# Expected: TRUE — chain blocked at Quality

# Test 2: Competency indep of Equip_Avail? (unconditional)
dseparated(rwanda_dag,
           "Competency", "Equip_Avail", c())
# Expected: TRUE — no connecting path

# Test 3: Competency indep of Equip_Avail given Quality? (collider)
dseparated(rwanda_dag,
           "Competency", "Equip_Avail", "Quality")
# Expected: FALSE — collider bias opens the path!
```

::: {.callout-box .green}
TRUE = independent (path blocked). FALSE = information flows. Test 3 shows the collider effect in action.
:::


## Step 4: Paths and Adjustment Sets

```{r}
#| label: paths-and-adjustments
#| echo: true

# All paths from CHW_Training to Neonatal_Mortality
paths(rwanda_dag, from = "CHW_Training", to = "Neonatal_Mortality")

# Testable predictions: if data violates any, revise the model
impliedConditionalIndependencies(rwanda_dag)

# What must we control for to estimate the causal effect?
adjustmentSets(rwanda_dag,
               exposure = "CHW_Training",
               outcome  = "Neonatal_Mortality")
# Returns {} — no confounders (CHW_Training is a root node)
```

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Why the empty set?** CHW_Training has no parents in this DAG, so there are no backdoor paths to close. The causal effect can be estimated without adjustment — *if* the DAG is correct.
:::


## Key Takeaways

::: {.key-takeaway}
**A qualitative causal model makes your assumptions visible, shareable, and testable.**

Every DAG is built from three triplets — **chains**, **forks**, and **colliders** — each with its own information flow rule.

Chains and forks: conditioning on the middle *blocks* the flow. Colliders: conditioning on the middle *opens* the flow. Get this backwards and you introduce bias instead of removing it.

For Rwanda: three investment decisions flow through three mediators into Quality of Care, then Neonatal Mortality. The diagram tells us *where* to look — the numbers (Chapter 4) will tell us *how much*.
:::
